title: Command Pattern
summary: Turning a request into an object so it can be queued, logged, or undone — the pattern behind undo/redo stacks, job queues, and macro recording.

slides.markdown:
**Command** turns "do this action" into an object instead of a direct method call. A text editor's toolbar button doesn't call `document.bold()` directly — it holds a `BoldCommand` object with an `execute()` method, and the button just calls `execute()` without knowing what it does.

That one indirection unlocks a lot: you can queue commands, log them, replay them, or pair each with an `undo()` to build an undo stack — none of which is possible if the button calls the method directly.

slides.sectionTitle: The problem: decoupling "what to do" from "when/who triggers it"
slides.markdown:
A toolbar's Bold button calls `document.applyBold()` directly. That's fine until you need the same action triggerable from a keyboard shortcut, a menu item, and a macro-recording feature — now three different triggers each need to know about `document` and call the exact right method with the right arguments.

It gets worse the moment you want undo: the button would need to remember not just what it did, but how to reverse it, and that knowledge doesn't belong in a UI button's click handler.

The underlying problem: the *trigger* (button, shortcut, menu) and the *action* (what actually happens) are different concerns that keep getting welded together, making every new trigger or requirement (logging, undo, queuing) a change to code that shouldn't need to know about any of that.

slides.sectionTitle: Command: encapsulate a request as an object with execute()
slides.markdown:
**Command** wraps a request — an action plus everything needed to perform it — into an object implementing a single-method interface, typically `execute()`. A `BoldCommand` holds a reference to the `document` (or the specific text range) and its `execute()` calls `document.applyBold(range)` internally.

The **invoker** (the button, the shortcut handler) only knows it holds a `Command` and calls `execute()` — it has zero knowledge of `document` or what "bold" even means. The **receiver** (`document`) is the object that actually does the work; the command just knows how to ask it correctly.

Because a command is now a real object, it can be stored, passed around, logged, or queued — none of which is possible with a bare method call.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: invoker to command to receiver, decoupled
slides.markdown:
The **invoker** (a button or shortcut) holds a `Command` reference and calls `execute()` on it. The **command** object holds a reference to the **receiver** (the object that does the real work) and, inside `execute()`, calls the receiver's actual method with the right arguments.

<<< Image: three boxes left to right — Invoker, Command, Receiver — with an arrow Invoker->Command labeled execute(), and an arrow Command->Receiver labeled the real action (e.g. applyBold(range)) >>>

The invoker never touches the receiver directly — it only ever calls `execute()` on whatever command it's holding, which is what lets the same button be rewired to a totally different action just by swapping which command it holds.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: an undoable Command with execute()/undo() for a text editor
Undo/redo stacks built from Command history
slides.markdown:
Once every action is a `Command` with `execute()` and `undo()`, undo/redo is just two stacks. Running a new command pushes it onto the **undo stack**. Undoing pops from the undo stack, calls `undo()`, and pushes that same command onto a **redo stack**. Redoing pops from the redo stack, calls `execute()` again, and pushes it back onto the undo stack.

This is why doing a *new* action after an undo clears the redo stack in most editors: the sequence of commands has branched, and replaying the old redo history no longer matches what's on screen.

The entire feature — a common ask in system-design interviews — reduces to "two stacks of objects that each know how to reverse themselves," which only works because Command turned actions into objects in the first place.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: Command vs Strategy — an action-plus-receiver vs an algorithm
slides.markdown:
| | Command | Strategy |
|---|---|---|
| What's encapsulated | A request: an action, its receiver, and its arguments | An algorithm: one interchangeable computation |
| Typical method | `execute()` (often paired with `undo()`) | A method that returns a computed result (`price()`, `sort()`) |
| Held state | Usually holds a specific receiver and specific arguments | Usually stateless — same strategy object reused across calls |
| Reason to use | Decouple triggering from doing; enable undo, queuing, logging | Decouple *which computation* runs from the code that needs a result |

**How to decide:** if you need to remember, replay, or reverse a specific past action, that's Command. If you just need to swap which computation produces a value right now, that's Strategy.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: commands holding stale receiver state, causing wrong undo behavior
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A command captures everything it needs at creation time, so `undo()` will always reverse exactly what `execute()` did."

**Why it's wrong:** if `BoldCommand` captures a `range` by reference (say, `[start: 10, end: 20]`) and the document's content shifts — text is inserted earlier in the document by a *different* command before this one is undone — that same numeric range now points at the wrong characters. `undo()` faithfully removes bold from whatever text is currently at positions 10-20, which may no longer be what was bolded.

**Correct model:** either make ranges resilient to shifts (anchors that move with edits, not raw indices), or have `execute()` snapshot exactly what it changed (not just the intent) so `undo()` restores that precise prior state, not a position that may have drifted.

slides.sectionTitle: Where this shows up: job queues, macro recording, GUI actions
slides.markdown:
**Job/task queues** (a background-jobs system like Sidekiq or a message queue consumer) are Command at scale — each job is a serialized command object with everything needed to execute it later, on a different machine, decoupled entirely from whatever enqueued it. **Macro recording** (recording a sequence of editor actions to replay later) is literally a list of Command objects captured and re-executed. **GUI toolkits** use Command as the standard way to wire buttons, menu items, and keyboard shortcuts to the same underlying action without duplicating the trigger-handling code three times.

The common thread: anywhere an action needs to be created in one place and executed in another — later, elsewhere, or repeatedly — Command is the pattern doing that separation.
